questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Wanted a good university in terms of academics, but also one somewhat near Danmark, in a compatible culture. I wanted good courses that I could learn from.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The process is not that complex, but ETH provided almost all information you need through emails, seminars and webinars. ETH was also helpful about adding/dropping and recommendations for workload, as well as recommendations of public transit rebates and such.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Asked the exchange office about distance exam. The ETH office was very helpful in this regard. KU not so much. It took 2 months even to get confirmation if it was possible. Once the request reached the examination office of KU however, it was quite nice from there, and they were very competent.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I got my housing through WOKO (which was in turn through ETH). Quite decent housing itself, and super nice social community. Very easy to apply, but you weren't guaranteed a spot.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
If you have to find private housing yourself, make sure to look outside of Zurich central. It is almost impossible to find housing there, and public transit is very reliable.

I would super recommend WOKO if you got an offer. Reasonable prices and nice social aspect. It can be somewhat hard to find local friends (especially in the beginning), so WOKO makes a lot of sense.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Quite scary to only get an answer whether I was homeless or not in July. Especially since it was (reportedly) quite hard to find housing private in Zurich.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The website for registration (myStudies) is quite old, but actually very functional, and does what it needs to do. You are neither prioritised nor deprioritised, so you can take essentially all courses (depending on restrictions from host department), but you also need to be fast if you want courses with restricted seats.

Understanding which courses are under which departments (based on which it is "offered in"), and finding actual courses to take could be quite hard, since you just got an unfiltered list of both MA and BSc courses to choose from, and there are a lot of courses

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could contact student administration, but the process itself was quite easy (while finding the courses was quite had)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all courses I registered/wanted for

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look at relevant degrees you can take at ETH (for instance comp-sci master and bachelor, robotics, computer engineering etc.). Each degree has several specialisations, which include variety of different courses. Thus you can get inspiration from those.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I did mostly MA by ECTS, but 2 of each. Generally courses are slightly harder than KU, with significantly harder (to pass and get 6.0 (top grade)). Most compsci courses are more math heavy and based on theory of computation than at KU, but they seem to have had less systems courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Lectures were to a larger extent seen as optional, and recording were almost always provided via their
video.ethz.ch
website (super nice). However, lectures were generally also seen as complementary to the reading material, so you would often have to read supplementary material to get the syllabus. However it depends on the exact course (e.g. COOP was 100% lecture slides as material).
I did feel that I got more out of the classes I took at ETH than I would at an average KU course. Exams were generally less fruitful however, and usually depended largely on memorisation, as well as cheatsheets. However they are still somewhat manageable, grading was usually quite lenient, and with enough studying it is definitely feasible to get high grades.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Compiler Design
- Computational Thinking
- Concepts of Object Oriented Programming (COOP)
- Advanced Machine Learning (AML)

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
COOP was super nicely taught with engaging lectures. Also very interesting material, and Prof. -NAME REDACTED- is probably the best professor i've ever had. Somewhat arbitrary exam, but also hard material to test in a classic end-of-year exam, and definitely doable. COOP's last year was my semester, but he said from 2027 there would be a new, similar course removing the object-oriented focus (since it was mostly already gone).

CompThi was not meant for computer science students, but actually gave a quite nice overview of some of the theoretical aspects of computing (such as N=NP). If you've had DIS and AD, about 1/3 of the syllabus is directly repeated, and the rest is quite simple. Would recommend the course in general, as the teaching was quite good.

Compiler Design was also super fun. 50% of grade was projects with a provided test suite, so getting a high project grade was quite easy. The projects were manageable and quite fun. Exam is somewhat hard in some aspects, but you could also get a lot of partial marks (and with some studying acing the exam is definitely not impossible).

I can't really recommend AML. The course was very disorganised, had a weird quiz element that took way longer to study for than it should (since it was while normal teaching and assignments were happening). The course does give a good understanding of current (almost-)cutting edge ML, and a very strong mathematical foundation on those models, but it rarely teaches you the math, and the math is really all you need for the exam. Unless you have a very strong Stats/Probability and Linear Algebra background, it is essentially a math course added onto the ML course. This also means "optimising" for the exam means you won't learn any/very little of the ML.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Food and especially takeout is super expensive. Meat in particular is super expensive, and a kebab is 110+. Public transit is quite reasonable if you buy a half-fare card (1 year coverage, half price on public transit for 800kr one time). However public transit is also super good. Health insurance is covered by EU.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Hiking trails and lifts for those is somewhat cheap compared to everything else in the country, but definitely worth it: the hikes are super beautiful. Beers as student bars is quite cheap, but beers out are more or less CPH level.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
ASVZ (student sport association) is free, and gives access to tons of both free courses (dance, basketball, group gym training, swimming etc.), and some paid where you pay to pay to rent equipment (like golf or fencing). It also provides free access to gyms on campus.

There are tons of clubs on campus. I went to the chess and CTF club a few times and met some super cool people. Would recommend checking out if any are your interests. They also have robotics and space and stuff.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join some ASVZ activities and some relevant clubs. Its more or less the only way to meet local students, since many courses are large and with little group work.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go hiking during the summer/fall. It really is super beautiful. Winters can be spent going to other nearby countries, both Flixbus and train is quite cheap to e.g. France and Italy.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. It is pretty similar to Denmark

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: You almost certainly much gotta have some common interest, like a club, or grouping up for an assignment. The master courses are very international, since many people come from both French speaking part of Switzerland and other countries, so people are generally more open and friendly in those.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They are pretty much as enclosed as Danish people.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: High trust based society and really a well-functioning country.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Take courses that you actually find interesting, and follow through the semester. The course load is pretty large, but manageable if you spread it out, and most courses are super interesting if you actually care for the subjects.

Go to some ASVZ activities and/or some clubs. Great way to meet people. Also recommend PapperlaPub in the CAB basement and Erasmus Student Network activities: super fun.

Check the prerequisites of the courses you're taking: not just by name, but also by the actual contents. E.g. intro to ML or linear algebra is quite more extensive than in KU

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The exams are pretty hard, but remember that the people actually attending are just normal people swell, so if most pass of the local students, you probably will too (if you spend the effort), most exams are graded quite lenient.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I met and the learning opportunities. I would also recommend trying to get a project if you can. I personally didn't, but the professors seemed very engaged in the project students, and it can be a great way to "pad" your ECTS across the year rather than all final exams.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: the exams (especially at advanced machine learning).

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
